name: Amira Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week starts at five in the morning on Tuesdays and Fridays, when I help at Mr Okafor's bakery on Station Road before lectures. I'm studying pharmacy, so I have chemistry, a module on how the body processes medicines, and a lab where we weigh powders very carefully. I live at home with my parents and my grandmother. After dinner I study at the dining table while my grandmother watches her programmes. On Sundays we go to the temple together, and that part of the week is mine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Is there anything you worry about when you think about the next three years?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My parents did not go to university, and they are proud, but there is no money to spare. The loan covers my fees. I earn about enough for books and the bus. I have saved less than a month of what I spend. I got in with average results, no scholarship, so I feel I must work twice as hard to justify the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say that is what I expected. Big promises, small results. I'd tell my friends there is no need to be afraid, and I would say it is better to keep studying hard than to chase every new thing. I would not post about it, that is not my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be relieved. I want a profession that is steady, where I can help my family, and this means nothing changes under my feet. But I am still worried about money, because my parents have the house and bills and I have my loan. That worry is there every day, with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep studying, keep the bakery shifts, and keep to my routine. I would try to get a pharmacy counter job on Saturdays, since it is closer to my degree. I would also keep giving a little to the temple, and be careful about my own spending. I would not try new technology if I do not need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but heavy with money thoughts. I like when things are predictable. That feeling is a comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about the machines already used in pharmacies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the university pharmacy there is a machine that counts tablets. It is fine, but a pharmacist still checks every box. I feel safer when a person checks. I would not trust a machine alone with someone's medicine, and I have never used AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your grandmother say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would say that work is honest, and that I should not worry about what other people have. She would say, do your work properly and the rest follows. She always says that. It helps, a little, when the bills come.

say: I'd tell friends there is no need to be afraid: **keep studying** hard.
I would not post about it, because that is **not my way**.
think: I'm relieved: I want a **steady profession** and nothing changes under my feet.
My real worry is **money**: my parents' bills and my loan, with or without AI.
do: Keep the **bakery shifts** and my study routine.
Look for a Saturday **pharmacy counter** job closer to my degree.
Be careful with **spending** and avoid new technology I do not need.
feel: **Steady**, but heavy with money thoughts; predictability is a comfort.
S0.quote: I feel safer when a person checks. I would not trust a machine alone with someone's medicine
fieldNote: Amira values **predictability** and is relieved by a world that stays the same.
She has **never used AI** and feels safer when a person checks medicine.
Her grandmother's advice on honest work steadies her, but the thin cushion keeps her uneasy.

steps.text: Keep the Tuesday and Friday morning bakery shifts
Look for a Saturday counter job at a pharmacy
Keep spending to books, bus fare and the temple

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say it is a big change, but we have seen change before. My grandfather came here with nothing and managed. I would say families and communities must stay close, and that young people should learn a skill, not just follow screens. I would be careful what I say publicly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I would be quite worried. Pharmacy is a thinking job: checking prescriptions, dosages, stock orders. These could go to software. If the pharmacy needs fewer pharmacists, then my degree is not the safe thing my family thinks. I would not say this to my parents, because it would frighten them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would work harder, and ask my tutors straight out which parts of pharmacy will still need a person. I would try to get hospital pharmacy experience, since they handle complicated cases. I would not start using AI tools, but I might ask a classmate to show me one. I would keep the bakery job and increase my savings slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a little ashamed to be anxious. My family sacrificed for this degree and I do not want to waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in a pharmacy might software take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking the prescription against the patient's other medicines, and ordering stock. A computer can check a prescription quickly. It cannot look at a worried old man and notice he has not understood the instructions. That is what I hope remains the pharmacist's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should look after people whose jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the community, then the government. My father says you should not wait for the state. If a neighbour loses work, the temple committee has helped before. I think that is better than handouts, but some help for people who have contributed all their life is fair.

say: I would say **families and communities** must stay close, and young people should learn a real skill.
I'd be careful about what I say **publicly**.
think: Pharmacy is a thinking job, so my degree may **not be as safe** as my family thinks.
I'd not tell my parents, because it would **frighten them**.
do: Ask tutors which parts of pharmacy still need a **person**.
Seek **hospital pharmacy** experience, where cases are complicated.
Ask a classmate to show me one **AI tool**, without promising to use it.
feel: **Anxious**, and a little ashamed to be anxious about my family's sacrifice.
S1.quote: A computer can check a prescription quickly. It cannot look at a worried old man and notice he has not understood the instructions.
fieldNote: Amira hides her worry from her **parents**, protecting their pride in her degree.
Her answer on **who helps** is traditional: family first, community next, state last.
She hesitates on AI but accepts she may need to see a tool shown by a classmate.

steps.text: Ask tutors which pharmacy tasks will still need a person
Add ten pounds a week to savings from the bakery
Ask a classmate to show me one AI tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say it is too fast and not right. A society needs time to look after its people. I would say politicians should slow it down, and employers should keep people on. I do not think it is for companies to decide on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I would be very frightened. Pharmacy is almost entirely thinking work, and I would be half-way through the degree. The bakery job might survive, but it would not pay the loan. My parents sacrificed everything and I might have nothing to give back. I could not sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would speak to my parents and grandmother first, and then to the tutors. I would hold on to the bakery job and take any extra hours. I would ask the temple elders if there is any help for students. I do not know how to use new technology, and I would be afraid to start, but I might have to learn the basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor is moving. I would try to be calm at home, but at night I would not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would sit them down on a Sunday after the temple, when everyone is calm. I would tell them truthfully, in simple words, that things are changing and I may need to change my plan. My father would be quiet. My mother would cry. My grandmother would say, we have survived worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the temple community do in a case like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would help, I think. People bring food, someone knows someone who is hiring. It is not a big organisation, but it works. Still, if a whole community is affected at once, there is less to give. That is what frightens me about two years.

say: I would say it is **too fast** and politicians should slow it down.
I'd say it is not for **companies** to decide on their own.
think: I'd be **very frightened**: pharmacy is mostly thinking work and I'd be half-way through.
My parents sacrificed everything and I might have **nothing to give back**.
do: Tell my parents and grandmother **truthfully** on a Sunday after the temple.
Hold the **bakery job** and take every extra hour.
Ask the **temple elders** about help for students.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the floor is moving, calm at home but not at night.
S2.quote: My father would be quiet. My mother would cry. My grandmother would say, we have survived worse.
fieldNote: Amira's fear is **relational**: she is more afraid of letting her parents down than of the technology.
The **community** idea is real support but she doubts it scales if everyone is hit at once.
Her resistance to technology leaves her with few new options, which raises alarm.

steps.text: Tell my parents and grandmother the truth after the temple
Take every extra bakery hour while it lasts
Ask the temple elders about help for students

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say that five years is enough if people act carefully. I would say we should teach children skills that last, like honesty, hard work and caring for each other, and not only how to use machines. I would not be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I would feel better but not safe. I would finish my degree in three years and have two years of work. Pharmacy may still be a profession then, maybe smaller. I would want to choose the part that needs trust, like talking to patients. I would also be afraid for my parents, who will be near retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would finish the degree, work in a pharmacy as soon as I can, and save every spare pound. I would train as a clinical pharmacist if the tutors say that part grows. I would learn some basic technology, but not rush it. I would also help my parents plan, because they will want to stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned, but less than before. It feels like a hard road that I can still walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do that two don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years would break me. Five years lets me finish and earn. I would have some savings and a profession on paper. That matters a lot to my family. They will measure it in whether I am settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about how you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop waiting for others to show me. I would sit down with a friend who uses these tools and learn one thing each week. I do not like it, but I would rather know what it does than be afraid of it.

say: I would say **five years** is enough if people act carefully.
I'd say children should be taught lasting skills: honesty, hard work and **caring** for each other.
think: I'd feel better but **not safe**: pharmacy may still exist, maybe smaller.
I'd be afraid for my **parents**, who will be near retirement.
do: Finish the degree and work in a **pharmacy** as soon as I can.
Train as a **clinical pharmacist** if tutors say that part grows.
Learn **one tool a week** from a friend, without rushing.
feel: **Concerned**, but less than before, like a hard road I can still walk.
S3.quote: Two years would break me. Five years lets me finish and earn. I would have some savings and a profession on paper.
fieldNote: Amira's relief is real but limited: five years gives **qualification**, not safety.
She names **trust** as the part of pharmacy a machine lacks.
Her resistance softens: she accepts learning one tool a week to avoid fear.

steps.text: Train as a clinical pharmacist if tutors say it grows
Save every spare pound from pharmacy work
Learn one new tool a week from a friend
Help my parents plan their retirement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years is a gift. A person can plan a whole career in that time. I would say we should use it to build skills and keep families strong. And I would say the government should not wait until the last year to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I would feel at peace. I would finish, work for a few years, maybe get married and have a family. By 2036 I would be a settled pharmacist, and hands-on care lasts longer. I would not be afraid for myself. I would worry about the young ones, my cousins, who might not find their way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would qualify, work, and save. I would learn what the profession needs along the way. I would help my cousins study and find honest work. I would build a home with my husband, if it is God's will. And I would be careful about technology, but not afraid of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. A quiet sort of hope, like at the temple on a calm Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years change about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach my children that a good job is honest, and that people matter more than machines. I would teach them to learn something with their hands and head. And that if the world changes, family is the thing that stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your own children one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop being so careful about every pound. For a few years I would only watch the bills. With ten years, I could afford to take a small risk, maybe a course in something new, because the ground would be steadier.

say: I would say ten years is **a gift**, and government should not wait until the last year.
I'd say we should use the time to build skills and **keep families strong**.
think: I'd feel **at peace**: a settled pharmacist by 2036, and hands-on care lasts longer.
I'd worry about the **young ones**, my cousins, who may not find their way.
do: Help my **cousins** study and find honest work.
Take a small **risk**, such as a course in something new, once the ground is steadier.
feel: **Hopeful**, a quiet hope like a calm Sunday at the temple.
S4.quote: I would teach my children that a good job is honest, and that people matter more than machines.
fieldNote: Amira's **traditional** values surface most with ten years: family, honest work, faith.
She finally contemplates a small **risk**, which signals how much time eases her.
Uneasy, not calm, because her cousins' futures and her own thin savings still weigh.

steps.text: Qualify as a pharmacist and save steadily from the first pay
Help my cousins study and find honest work
Take a short course in something new once settled

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time to finish, no way to pay my family back. What would help is honest guidance from the university, a small hardship fund, and employers that keep people on while this settles. I would also like the temple and the family to know what is happening so that I am not carrying it alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that we are not afraid of work. We are afraid of being left with nothing to show for it. Give us a fair chance to finish what we started.

headlineQuote: We are not afraid of work. We are afraid of being left with nothing to show for it.
portrait: Amira is **19**, a first-year pharmacy student who helps at a bakery at dawn and lives with her parents and grandmother.
She is traditional, faith-minded and **resistant** to technology; she has never used AI and trusts a person to check medicine.
Her fear is about **letting her family down**: they sacrificed for her degree and she hides worry from them.
Her mood goes from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, and eases with ten years to plan.
She turns to **family and the temple** before the state, and softens only slowly on learning new tools.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries her most, because she would be half-way through with nothing to repay her family.
whatWouldHelp: Honest guidance from the university, a small **hardship fund** and employers who keep people on while things settle.
